big_idea: Companies facing disruption shouldn't choose between defending their current business and building a new one -- they need to run both transformations simultaneously, repositioning the core for resilience while separately building a new growth engine, connected by a shared capabilities link.

tool.label: The Dual Transformation Framework (Transformation A / Transformation B)
tool.text: Transformation A repositions the core business to maximize its resilience as its industry shifts, reallocating investment even if it means cutting product lines. Transformation B builds a new, separate growth engine based on a genuinely different business model, run outside the core organization's existing structure and metrics. The capabilities link is the deliberate mechanism connecting the two -- identifying which hard-to-replicate assets from the core can accelerate Transformation B without letting B's different pace destabilize A.
tool.note: Because the framework requires running two very differently-paced organizational efforts at once with real executive attention split between them, under-resourcing either side is a common failure mode the book flags but doesn't fully solve for resource-constrained companies.

ideas.title: Repositioning is not retreat
ideas.text: Transformation A is framed as proactively reallocating a still-valuable core business's resources toward its most durable segments, not managing decline.

ideas.title: Structural separation for Transformation B
ideas.text: New-growth efforts need their own metrics, incentives, and often physical separation from the core to avoid being judged by the wrong yardsticks.

ideas.title: The capabilities link as competitive moat
ideas.text: The specific assets transferred between A and B are what make dual transformation defensible rather than just running two unrelated businesses.

ideas.title: Sequencing and timing
ideas.text: Waiting until the core business visibly declines to start Transformation B is typically too late, given how long new engines take to reach scale.

ideas.title: Leadership's split-attention problem
ideas.text: CEOs must personally sponsor both transformations, since middle management alone can't resolve the resource conflicts between them.

ideas.title: Case-based validation
ideas.text: Drawing on real companies (Adobe, Netflix's shift from DVD to streaming) rather than purely theoretical modeling.

try_it: List which parts of your current core business deserve more investment vs. which are candidates for reduction, as a first Transformation A pass.
Identify one nascent growth bet currently being evaluated by the same metrics as the core business, and propose separate success metrics for it.
Name one hard-to-replicate asset your core business has that a new-growth effort could legitimately borrow.
Set a specific trigger point that would tell you it's time to start a Transformation B effort.
best_for: Executives at established, mid-to-large companies facing visible industry disruption who need to fund innovation without abandoning a still-profitable core.
Corporate innovation and strategy teams looking for a structured model for running an internal venture alongside the main business.
less_useful: Early-stage startups or small businesses with no legacy core to reposition.
Readers wanting quantitative, ROI-driven guidance on how to split limited capital between A and B.

related.why: Blue Ocean Strategy shares the same instinct to build genuinely new value rather than compete head-on.
Good Strategy/Bad Strategy offers complementary diagnostic rigor for deciding what the core should keep.
